pass_a_gloss: What need is there for my silence, which many others have often, but I especially now, being willing and unwilling, being forced to be silent and to keep silent. For I have neglected and I am ignorant of these good and fine words, which are spoken or composed by the chosen and approved names and verbs in a certain uninterrupted sequence. I, being less capable of this pleasant Greek work. But this eight-year period is already mine, during which I have not myself either said or written anything great or small, nor have I heard from another who has written or said something, either in private or in public, offering panegyric and competitive speeches, except for these wonderful men who have possessed fine philosophy, to whom elegance and simplicity of names are less important. But putting their voices second, they wish to examine and proclaim each of their own works with precision. I do not think they do not want to, but they want very much the good and precise things of thoughts to be poured out and expressed in speech. But perhaps they are not able, having the power at hand in their thoughts, the sacred and divine and fine word in their expressions, to grasp each of two men's abundance, and this human and small soul, being very contrary. If indeed silence is somehow a friend and helper to the mind and discovery. But the eloquent man, you will not find anywhere else, except in voices and the continuous practice of these. And the mind takes hold of another kind of learning, and the mouth binds the tongue, if I wanted to say something, even small, to the Greek voice, our wonderful men, to whom now all the things under human rule are directed, not being hindered or learning effortlessly, being themselves accurate and poetic and wonderful, and being called most Greek, having been expressed and handed down to the Roman voice, which is persuasive and boastful and conforming to the royal authority, but burdensome to me. But in no other way is it possible or desirable for me. But since our words are nothing other than certain images of the passions of our soul, to those who are able to speak, like certain good painters and skilled craftsmen, who are most skilled in their art, but unskilled in the material of colors, we would agree that they write not only similar, but also varied and very beautiful writings, with the mixture of flowers, without being hindered in anything.
pass_b_english: I am compelled to silence, a state that many others have often experienced, but which is especially mine now, whether I like it or not. For I have neglected the study of fine and elegant words, which are spoken or written in a particular sequence by those who are skilled in the use of language. I must admit that I am not well-suited to this kind of Greek eloquence. However, for the past eight years, I have not spoken or written anything of significance, nor have I heard anyone else do so, except for those remarkable individuals who have mastered the art of fine philosophy, and for whom the elegance and simplicity of language are of little concern. Instead, they focus on examining and proclaiming their ideas with precision, and they do so with great enthusiasm, pouring out their thoughts and expressing them in speech. Perhaps, though, they are not able to grasp the full range of human experience, with all its complexities and contradictions, and to convey it in their words. If silence can be a helpful companion to the mind and a catalyst for discovery, then the ability to speak eloquently is a gift that can only be developed through practice and dedication. Moreover, the pursuit of knowledge and understanding can be a powerful force, one that can shape our thoughts and our words, and even influence the way we express ourselves. Our leaders, who are so skilled in the art of rhetoric, and who have been trained in the ways of Greek eloquence, now direct the affairs of the world, unencumbered by obstacles, and with effortless ease. They are masters of the Roman language, which is so persuasive and boastful, and yet, to me, it is a burden. But I suppose that this is just the way things are, and that there is no other way to be. Since our words are merely reflections of our inner lives, and of the passions that drive us, then those who are skilled in the art of language are like painters, who use their craft to create beautiful and varied works of art, unencumbered by any limitations, and with a deep understanding of the nuances of the human experience.

review.notes: Pass B introduces significant content not present in the Greek source, violating the rule against adding to the text. Specifically, Pass B adds entire sentences/clauses regarding the 'pursuit of knowledge and understanding' and 'shaping our thoughts' which are not in the Greek: 'Moreover, the pursuit of knowledge and understanding can be a powerful force, one that can shape our thoughts and our words, and even influence the way we express ourselves.' It also adds 'with a deep understanding of the nuances of the human experience' at the end, which is not in the Greek. Additionally, Pass B misinterprets the Greek regarding the 'Roman voice' (Ῥωμαίων φωνῇ) by calling it the 'Roman language', whereas the Greek refers to the voice/speech of the Romans. Pass A is a more faithful translation but the failure of Pass B necessitates a fail.
reasons: Pass B adds substantial theological/philosophical commentary not found in the Greek source: 'Moreover, the pursuit of knowledge and understanding can be a powerful force, one that can shape our thoughts and our words, and even influence the way we express ourselves.'
